Long hauls are part of the deal in North Texas. Six hours in a trailer, a run the next morning, haul home Sunday. Your horse doesn't get a recovery week — he gets a gate check and a pat.

Here's what soreness looks like after a hard trip:

— Tight through the loin, short on the hip swing
— Stride that looks lazy but doesn't fix with warm-up
— Ears back or flinching at the cinch

None of that is attitude. None of it is age. That's a horse telling you something is locked up.

Dr. Leo comes to your barn — no trailering a sore horse, no added stress. He checks the spots that take the most abuse on a hard-hauling performance horse and gets them moving right.

One of the most common questions Dr. Leo gets at North Texas barns: 'How often should we do this?'

Honest answer — it depends on the horse and what you're asking of him.

Here's the general framework:

— Competing most weekends: every 4 to 6 weeks
— Heavy haul schedule or multiple runs a week: every 3 to 4 weeks
— Off-season or light work: every 6 to 8 weeks

The goal isn't to keep your horse adjusted forever. It's to keep him from building up the kind of compensation pattern that shows up as a bad barrel, a slow stop, or a lead you can't get.

Consistent maintenance costs less than fixing a horse that's been crooked for six months.
